text: the stairwell. Desks stacked against shelving units stacked against lockers, the whole mass of stuff settling into the stairwell opening like it had grown there. Some pieces looked warped. Wet. Some wedged. Some clearly just tossed. All crammed into the stairwell as if the building had tried to eat itself. The furniture was preschool sized mostly, but there was enough of it packed in that the combined weight was something else entirely. There was no space to squeeze through. No handholds. Overhead, the lone light in the ceiling dimmed with a jittery flicker before settling into its usual brightness. "That's what he was doing," Dwight murmured, mostly to himself. The scraping sounds from upstairs when they first came in. Danny throwing things around. They'd assumed boredom. They hadn't been wrong, exactly. David was already at the stack, shoulder against the nearest locker, pushing. The locker didn't move. He reset his footing and pushed harder. The furniture shifted — just slightly, a quarter inch of give — and then settled back exactly as it had been, as if the gap had never existed. David stared at it, dumfounded. Pushed again. Same result. He tried a desk next, getting his fingers under the edge and hauling upward. The desk rocked once and came back down with a muffled sound that the air swallowed before it could properly echo, and David pulled his shoulder back with a sharp exhale, rolling it once. "Brilliant. Just... great. The hell even IS this?” “More importantly, how’d we not hear it? This should have made a ton of noise. We couldn’t have been more than 50 feet away. Tops. I know the hallway eats sound in the corners, but there should have been something.” They tried to clear the stairs, pulling one chair, then another, but everything they dislodged seemed to drag more with it. Like the pile was settling, not shrinking. Several of the heavier pieces wouldn’t budge at all. He took a breath and shoved again. The metal scraped, and the sound came out small, politely swallowed by the air. He stepped back with a scowl and flexed his fingers. Dwight tried a chair leg, then another, testing angles for leverage. The sounds were wrong. That was the thing that kept nagging at Dwight as the two worked methodically through their options — wrong in a specific, deliberate way. When David's shoulder connected with the locker, the impact made a sound that didn't carry. When the furniture shifted and settled back, the scrape of it was swallowed before it could reach the walls. The basement should have been bouncing noise around, hard floors and concrete and all that pipe — instead everything just landed flat, absorbed, like the air itself had decided sound wasn't worth keeping. Dwight stood in the water and listened to the silence eating itself for a moment longer. He almost mentioned it, then thought better of it. David already looked like he was getting annoyed with the stairway plug. Bringing up one more bit of weirdness in all this was not likely to land in his favor. Dwight glanced back the way they came. “Should we go back? Danny gets bored easily; maybe he moved?” David looked back at him over his shoulder, expression unreadable. "Worth checking," Dwight murmured lightly, with slightly less conviction. David nudged a shelf with his boot, barely listening, then hissed a breath through his teeth and shook his foot as if something in the water had touched him. “Nope. Don’t like that.” Dwight looked through the mouth of the pipe hall again. The corridor lurched longer while he watched it — only a fraction, only the kind of shift you can blame on a blink. Looking back to try and get David’s attention again, he noticed the stiffness in his shoulders and realized he had seen it too. The decision settled around them both. It was time to go. Now. That was when the pipes screamed. Somewhere deeper down the pipe hall, something ruptured — a sharp concussive crack followed immediately by a sustained shriek of pressure, the sound of it tearing through the basement — and both of them ducked on instinct, water soaking into clothing and rippling against random debris around them, Dwight's hands finding the nearest pipe junction, David crouched low with his arms thrown over his head, both of them braced for something that didn't come. Steam burst out from a seam to their left and hit the ceiling in a white bloom that didn’t disperse correctly. The bulb above them stuttered as if it had hiccupped on its own heat. Once. Twice. The third time, it simply failed, plunging the entire basement into an oppressive darkness. The building held its breath. Chapter Two – Floodline Darkness fell and did not lift. There was no flicker. No emergency backup. No lingering hum of standby power. One moment, the overhead light buzzed, warped and sickly, and the next, it was gone. The darkness just was — thick and absolute, a total absence that clung to their skin like wet cloth, pressing in from all sides until the two of them were just breathing in it and trying to remember where the walls were. Dwight couldn’t tell where his skin stopped and the world began. The water had reached his shins, warm in a way that felt wrong — closer to body temperature than anything a basement had a right to be. A splash to his right; David swore under his breath, reaching out for something solid to orient himself, and caught his shoulder hard on a locker. The sound it made was flat and brief and immediately gone. The water sloshed violently at the impact, licking up Dwight’s calves and soaking the fabric that hadn’t already glued to him. “You good?” Dwight called into the void. “Peachy,” David grunted. “Don’t suppose you’ve got a light?” Dwight patted his jacket, and his fingers bumped the slim cylinder tucked in the inside pocket.
